problems.stem: A module replaces three static text screens with three flip-card animations containing the same words. What is the most likely effect on learning?
options: Learning improves because the content is now interactive.
Learning is unlikely to improve, because the flips add motion but require no new thinking from the learner.
Learning improves because animation always increases engagement.
Learning declines only if the cards load slowly.
problems.explanation: Interaction is instructional only when it drives generative processing. Flipping a card to reveal identical text adds motion, not cognitive work.

problems.stem: For categorizing 8 examples into 3 groups, a designer invents a custom two-finger swipe gesture instead of using a familiar tabbed sort. When is the custom gesture justified?
options: Always, because custom interactions make the module memorable.
Only when the familiar tabbed pattern genuinely fails the task, since a familiar pattern lets learners spend attention on content rather than on learning the interface.
Never; instructional software must avoid all gestures.
Whenever the design team finds tabs visually boring.
problems.explanation: Familiar interaction patterns reduce extraneous load by reusing prior interface knowledge. Reserve novel patterns for cases where the familiar one cannot do the job.

problems.stem: A drag-and-drop step lets learners place molecules into bonding slots, but after dropping, the screen never changes and no hint appears. What is missing from the interaction pattern?
options: A scoreboard showing the class ranking.
A visible consequence: the loop never closes because the learner sees no result, hint, or change after acting.
A second drag-and-drop step on the same screen.
problems.explanation: Every learning interaction needs a visible consequence so the loop closes. Input without response is a decorative pattern, not an instructional one.

problems.stem: You must defend choosing a simple tabbed comparison over an animated 3D model for showing two protein shapes. Which justification is the strongest evidence-based revision note?
options: The tabs render faster than the 3D model.

Pilot eye-tracking showed learners spent 40 percent of time rotating the 3D model and never compared the shapes; the tabs put both shapes side by side so attention went to the comparison the task requires.
Tabs are the most common pattern on the web.
problems.explanation: The defensible note ties the pattern choice to evidence (eye-tracking) and to the cognitive demand of the task (comparison), not to speed or appearance.
